title: Goal mode
description: You set a goal and criteria, the agent works toward it step by step, and every step is closed with proof.

steps.question: “Make a shopping list and set a reminder for tonight.” How does the agent know it really finished, and didn't just say “done”?
steps.answer: By completion criteria: a goal has conditions that can be checked, and a step counts only when a condition is backed by proof. That is Goal mode, which the app calls Goal.

steps.text: In Plan mode, you approve a plan and wait for it to be carried out. In Goal mode, you set a goal and criteria for “done,” and the agent breaks it into steps on its own and works toward it, checking the result as it goes.

steps.imagePrompt: A small robot hiker walks a winding path toward a flag on top of a hill, checking a compass at each turn, with no map in its hands.
steps.caption: The goal is clear, the path is not: the agent checks at every step

steps.text: The main thing in Goal mode isn't the plan, it's the check: after every step, the engine compares the result with the criteria and moves on only then.

steps.definition: A checkable condition for “the task is closed,” set together with the goal. The engine checks it after every step and does not take the agent's word for it: it needs proof.
steps.example: “Done when there is both a shopping list and a reminder for tonight” — two checkable items.

steps.text: Inside a step, the agent runs the familiar ReAct rounds: think → do → look. When the step ends, the engine compares the result with the criteria. Confirmed means on to the next step. If not, the step is tried again.
Sound familiar? It's the same ReAct loop, only with a finish line: after each step we ask “are we at the goal?” instead of just running rounds.

steps.instruction: Put one step of Goal mode in order:
items: Check the result against the criteria
Decide: the step is closed, or try again
steps.explain: Action → check against the criteria → decision. And so on, step by step, until the goal is reached.

steps.text: Who does the checking? Not the model on its word. The engine closes a step with proof: a tool's result, a fact in memory, or your confirmation. The model's own assessment is the fallback and the weakest option: Muse Spark reasons before each answer, but it too likes to say “done” too soon.

steps.template: So that a step doesn't loop forever, Goal mode has a limit of ___ per step

steps.text: By default it is three rounds per step, and you can change it in Settings: “Goal mode: round limit.” If a step hits the limit, it becomes blocked and waits for you. If the rounds were enough but there's no proof, the step is tried again, up to two attempts in all. The agent doesn't hide this behind “done”: the plan card shows what got stuck.

steps.caption: Set the limit to 1 round and to 3, and compare how each one ends. The numbers are just an example

steps.situation: The task: “figure out why I spent more than usual this month.”
options: Goal mode: the steps can't be listed in advance
Plan mode: any analysis starts with a plan
Neither: the model can answer with no tools
steps.explain: How many times to look at the spending and where to dig will only become clear along the way. The path is unknown, and that is Goal mode's profile.

steps.text: Practice. Goal mode is only available for agents you build yourself. Build one with “Create agent” (Agents → Create agent): in the chat with the Builder, give it the Memory and Reminders tools, then on the “Review your agent” screen, in the Modes section, tick Goal and publish. In a chat with that agent, choose Goal and give it a task with a criterion, for example: “make a shopping list for borscht and set a reminder for tonight; done when there is both a list and a reminder.” A plan card arrives first. Tap “Approve,” and the steps go on by themselves in the background, with their replies appearing in this same chat. “Open →” shows the steps, their statuses and the proof.

Under the hood, Goal runs on the same engine as Plan mode: a plan of steps with statuses, where every criterion is closed with proof you can see on the plan card. You can also nudge it by hand: a new message in Goal mode immediately runs one more step. The “done means proven” rule is covered in detail in the Structured plans lesson.

To sum up. Plan mode is a gate: plan → wait for your “OK” → carry out. Goal mode is a goal with criteria: the agent works toward it step by step, and the engine counts a step only with proof. If it's clear what to do step by step, use Plan mode. If the goal and the way to check “done” are clear but the path is not, use Goal mode.

questions.q: How is Goal mode different from Plan mode?
options: Goal mode checks each step; Plan mode gates the start
It isn't: they are two names for the same mode
Goal mode uses no tools, it only reasons
questions.explain: Plan mode is a gate before the work. Goal mode is a path to a goal, with every step checked.

questions.q: What does the engine close a goal step with?
options: Proof: a tool's result or your “yes”
The model's word “done,” since it knows best
A timer: the set time passed, so the step is closed
questions.explain: A step counts on proof: a tool's result, a fact in memory or your confirmation. The model's own assessment is the fallback and the weakest option.

questions.q: What happens if a step hits the round limit?
options: The step is blocked and waits for you, as the card shows
The agent writes “done” and moves on
The loop keeps going, the limit doesn't matter
questions.explain: The round limit applies per step. When a step hits it, the step is blocked, and the plan card shows that instead of hiding it behind “done.”
